title: Module 10 — Waterproofing
text: Week of Nov 16 · Paired lecture: Multirotors

title: Module 10 — Waterproofing
text:
What you build today
A potted PCB, a lubricated and sealed gearbox, and a robot that survives a static immersion test.






WarningSilicone cure time gates this module



The PCB potting takes 12–24 hours to cure because of the depth. Plan the module so potting happens first and soldering happens after the cure, or across two sittings.

title: Module 10 — Waterproofing
text:
Before you arrive







Parts
Waterproofing box, Kapton tape, silicone sealant, USB-C cable, CorrosionX, white lithium grease


Tools
Needle, soldering iron


Read
This whole page before starting — the ordering matters

title: Module 10 — Waterproofing
text:
Flight controller waterproofing
First ensure that the FC fits within the 3D box before anything else.

Tape the bottom side of the box with Kapton.
Fill the bottom of the box with silicone sealant until it reaches the USB port hole.
Carefully slide the PCB assembly in, with the Seeeduino facing the bottom of the box.
Very important! Insert a USB-C cable into the port. This keeps the sealant from flowing into the port, and the cable is a convenient point to hold the assembly by.
Add sealant along the three free edges to fill any gaps, until the sealant reaches the level of the top side of the PCB. The PCB components and contacts should be left exposed.
Let the silicone cure — because of the depth this takes about 12–24 h.
Solder the wires and contacts.
Solder the voltage regulator.
Seal the top side of the PCB. The best method here is unclear. Tested solutions:

Nail polish
Silicone sealant
422C silicone conformal coating (datasheet)

title: Module 10 — Waterproofing
text:
ESC waterproofing
The ESC is potted the same way as the flight controller: it sits in its own 3D-printed frame, which is then filled with Silcoset so only the wire exits remain open. Figure 1 shows the three pieces together — motor, bare ESC, and the potted frame.






Figure 1: The motor, the ESC and the potted frame. The dark block is the frame filled with Silcoset; the ESC drops into it before the fill so the board ends up fully encapsulated with only the phase and signal wires leaving.









ImportantTo be completed by the instructor



The written procedure for this step, to the level of detail the flight controller has above: fill order, how the phase wires are held clear while the compound cures, cure time for this depth, and whether the ESC is potted before or after the motor wires are soldered in Module 3.

title: Module 10 — Waterproofing
text: Battery waterproofing

title: Module 10 — Waterproofing
text: Battery connector waterproofing

title: Module 10 — Waterproofing
text:
Gearbox
By default the gearbox on the FAAV4 robot is not waterproof at all, and it is normal for it to end up completely filled with water once submerged. Over years of use the gearbox proved resistant to fresh water with the factory lubricant. If that is removed/cleaned, then use the right lubricant below. The best is to avoid opening the gearbox and cleaning the gears.






WarningUse the right lubricant



A mix of CorrosionX and white lithium grease. Several dives have since been performed with the same gearbox that previously corroded, and it now runs smoothly.


Parts that rust: sun gear, planet gears, ring gear, planet shafts. Parts that do not: screws, motor shaft, washers, body, circlip.






NoteCheckpoint



PCB fully cured and potted with contacts exposed, gearbox lubricated and reassembled with the shaft bearing fitted, connector back-shell sealed, and a static immersion test passed with no ingress.

title: Module 8 — Tail and housing
text:
Housing
Use a foam cutter to cut an exterior housing for the FAAV. This is an important step for external tests: it adds a layer of protection and ensures the FAAV floats. Leave space for GPS and antenna insertions if you are using them.
To keep the FAAV level when floating — which helps visibility and getting it out of the water — it is recommended to put a certain amount of foam on the tail.

Choosing a foam
Various foams have been tested, with tradeoffs:









Foam
Floatability
Absorption
Impact behaviour




Extruded polystyrene (XPS)
Best, low density
Zero
Relatively brittle; little help damping landings


Closed-cell polyethylene (PE)
Decent, relatively low density
Light
Much more compliant; usable as protection



If someone ever has time, a multi-material housing could have its use cases.






WarningCheck solvent compatibility before painting or gluing foam



Some foams are very sensitive to solvents. Epoxy is inert and can act as glue.

title: Module 4 — Closed-loop control and tuning

title: Module 4 — Closed-loop control and tuning
text:
What you build today
The gearbox installed with a marker flag on the output, the Seeeduino wired in and commanding the ESC untethered, running continuously, then holding position, then tracking a velocity setpoint with a tuned loop.

title: Module 4 — Closed-loop control and tuning
text:
Before you arrive



Parts
Motor with shaft and sun gear from Module 2, Faulhaber 23.04:1 gearbox, M2.5×10 screws, 3D-printed plates, second vertical bracket, 3× M2.5 and 3× M2 screws, ESC from Module 3, 4x8 mm flanged bearing, Seeeduino XIAO nRF52840, its 3D-printed bracket, 3 wires


Tools
Bench supply with current limit, tachometer or camera, soldering iron


Read
This page in full - the speed limits below explain most of what you will hit

title: Module 4 — Closed-loop control and tuning
text:
Reduction
The motor is connected via a custom shaft to a gearbox with a 23.04:1 reduction by Faulhaber.1 Both parts are held in place by 3D-printed plates. The output shaft of the gearbox has its own bearing on the inside of the gearbox, and is also supported mid-way on the shaft by a 4×8 mm flanged bearing. This leaves 5 mm of shaft length free for the crank to be mounted on. A flat on the shaft helps lock the rotation of the M3 screw extending through the crank.






Motor shaft







Faulhaber gearbox






Installing the reduction
Our sun gear is already pressed onto the motor shaft from Module 2. What is left is mating the gearbox to the motor and fixing the pair to the plates.

Slide the gearbox onto the motor shaft so the sun gear engages the planets. It should seat with light hand pressure, if it resists, back off and check the sun gear is square on the shaft rather than forcing it.
Fix the blue part of the gearbox: the custom screws that come with the gearbox on one side, and M2.5×10 screws on the other.
Check the output turns freely by hand through a full revolution before applying power.
Close the gearbox: the silver part threads onto the blue part. Don’t tighten it.
Attach the second vertical bracket to the silver part of the gearbox with 3 × M2.5 screws.
Secure that bracket to the bottom fuselage plate with 3 × M2 screws. The motor bracket from Module 2 is already on the same plate, so between them the two brackets set the alignment of the whole drivetrain. Check the output still turns freely once both are bolted down.

title: Module 4 — Closed-loop control and tuning
text:
Onboard microcontroller
So far every command has come from your laptop over micro-USB. That works on the bench and nowhere else, a robot that has to move cannot stay tethered. The commander interface does not change; what changes is who talks to it. From here on the Seeeduino XIAO nRF52840 rides on the robot and sends those same commands, and your laptop talks to the Seeeduino instead of to the ESC.






Figure 1: The Seeeduino XIAO nRF52840. TX and RX are the two pads at the bottom corners — those are the ones you solder to, and they cross over to the ESC’s RX and TX respectively. The board is 21 × 17.5 mm, which is why it can ride on the robot at all.




Solder the Seeeduino and the ESC’s Serial1: TX, RX and GND lines. In Serial communication, TX and RX are crossed, each board’s transmit line goes to the other’s receive line, as drawn in the wiring diagram in Module 3. GND is not optional: without a shared reference the two boards have no agreed voltage for what counts as a high or low bit. To do this step, you will need to desolder the existing Serial1 TX RX lines to the daughterboard.
Install the Seeeduino in its 3D-printed bracket and into the robot.
Load the barebone Arduino sketch onto the Seeeduino — see Software for the repository.
Modify the sketch to spin the motor at 100 rad/s and confirm it on the flag you mounted on the gearbox output.







WarningYou lose the micro-USB serial link



Serial1 now goes to the Seeeduino rather than to the daughterboard, so the serial console you used in Module 3 stops working. Flashing the ESC still works — programming runs over SWD, on different pins — but every command and every value you read back now has to pass through the Seeeduino.
Plan for it: anything you still want to inspect over micro-USB, inspect before you solder these three wires.








ImportantTo be completed by the instructor



Which repository holds the barebone Seeeduino sketch, and on which branch. The nRF52 repositories currently in Software are marked outdated, so students following this page have nothing to clone.

title: Module 4 — Closed-loop control and tuning
text:
Task sequence

Mount a small flag on the gearbox output so rotation is visible and countable.
Achieve continuous spinning at low speed.
Achieve position control - the output holds against a hand disturbance.
Tune the loop and characterise your maximum usable speed.







ImportantTo be completed by the instructor



The specific PID tuning exercise, the target performance, and the sign-off criteria are course material and are not in the manufacturing guide.

title: Module 4 — Closed-loop control and tuning
section: Why low speed is the hard part
text:
Why low speed is the hard part
Regular drone ESCs start losing synchronisation at low speed, which is exactly the regime used for water propulsion. That is the reason this course uses an FOC ESC rather than a hobby unit — see Design notes.

title: Module 4 — Closed-loop control and tuning
text:
Going beyond 600 rad/s
Two issues limit speed: the micro-controller loop rate, and delays from the rotation sensor. Using SPI at 10 MHz and an AS5047P sensor rated for 28kRPM speeds are the required hardware changes that improves on delay. But at very high speeds, sensor lag still becomes the binding constraint, and shows up as high current draw and noise. We need to update the sensor electrical angle offset as a function of speed.

Sensor lag
Compensating sensor lag as speed increases is necessary to go above 600 rad/s without wasting current. It is currently hand-tuned every 100 rad/s, and a fitted function is used on the robot. This could be automated by ramping through the speeds and minimising phase current — future work. This SimpleFOC forum thread is useful on the topic.






NoteCheckpoint



Continuous rotation resulting in frequencies of 1 Hz all the way to 8 Hz without loss of synchronisation, position hold against a hand disturbance, and a recorded loop frequency from F. Do not exceed 8 Hz.




MCU speed
The goal is to maximise main loop frequency, which reached 13 kHz. Read the current loop frequency with the commander’s F command.







Change
Effect




motor.motion_downsample = 3
+0.8 kHz loop frequency


Disable monitoring
+0.2 kHz


Switch to SVPWM
No improvement observed. May help, unconfirmed


L = 0.0001
Tuning the inductance value helped — made voltage mode work much better

title: Module 2 — Motor and transmission shaft

title: Module 2 — Motor and transmission shaft
text:
What you build today
A brushless motor with a custom shaft pressed into its rotor bell, with the sun gear and the sensor magnet installed, bolted to its bracket and mounted on the motor plate. The gearbox itself goes on in Module 4.

title: Module 2 — Motor and transmission shaft
text:
Before you arrive



Parts
AS2303 KV1500 motor with pre-machined bell, custom motor shaft, sun gear from the Faulhaber 23.04:1 gearbox, 6 × 2.5 mm diametric magnet, 3D-printed magnet bracket, vertical nylon motor bracket, bottom fuselage plate, mounting screws


Tools
Circlip pliers, manual arbor press, superglue, hex drivers


Read
This page, and the Motor shaft section below in full before touching the motor. Brushless motors for the background

title: Module 2 — Motor and transmission shaft
text:
The motor — AS2303 KV1500
The AS2303 is a brushless outrunner. Read Brushless motors first.

We use the AS2303 KV1500 motor throughout the course. Its propeller horn cannot be separated from the bell, it has to be machined off in a lathe. That work, and the custom shaft, are prepared for you before the session.

What the KV rating means
KV is the motor’s velocity constant, quoted in rpm per volt. It says how fast the rotor spins per volt applied, with no load on the shaft:
\[\omega_0 = k_V \, U \tag{1}\]
The constant is not a marketing number — it falls out of the motor’s physics. As the rotor turns, its magnets sweep past the windings and induce a voltage that opposes the supply (the back-EMF):
\[U_\text{emf} = \frac{\omega}{k_V} \tag{2}\]
The supply voltage splits between this back-EMF and the ohmic drop across the winding resistance \(R\), so \(U = U_\text{emf} + R\,I\) and the speed under load becomes
\[\omega = k_V \left( U - R\,I \right) \tag{3}\]
which is why Equation 1 only holds at \(I \approx 0\). Draw current and the motor slows down.
The same constant fixes the torque. Electrical power in equals mechanical power out, \(U_\text{emf} I = \tau \omega\), and substituting Equation 2 gives \(\tau = I / k_V\) in SI units. Converting \(k_V\) from rpm/V to rad/s/V:
\[k_T = \frac{60}{2\pi \, k_V} \approx \frac{9.55}{k_V}
\qquad \text{with} \qquad \tau = k_T \, I \tag{4}\]
with \(k_T\) in N·m/A when \(k_V\) is in rpm/V. Torque and speed constants are inverses of each other. A high-KV motor spins fast but gives little torque per amp; a low-KV motor of the same size and mass does the opposite. You cannot buy both — you choose where on that trade-off to sit, and then recover the missing torque with a reduction.


What this means for our robot
With \(k_V = 1500\) rpm/V and a 4S LiPo at its 14.8 V nominal voltage:
\[\omega_0 = 1500 \times 14.8 = 22\,200 \ \text{rpm}
\qquad
k_T = \frac{9.55}{1500} = 6.4 \ \text{mN·m/A}\]
6.4 mN·m/A is very little torque, too little to drive the wings directly, which is exactly why the 23.04:1 Faulhaber gearbox is there. It multiplies torque by 23.04 and divides speed by the same factor. One revolution of the gearbox output is one full flapping cycle, so
\[f_\text{flap} = \frac{\omega}{60 \, r}
= \frac{22\,200}{60 \times 23.04} = 16.1 \ \text{Hz} \tag{5}\]
at no load. Under real aerodynamic and hydrodynamic loading the drive tops out near 15 200 rpm, i.e. about 11 Hz of flapping, the figure you will see again in Module 4.

title: Module 2 — Motor and transmission shaft
text:
Motor shaft
To pair the motor with the gearbox, the stock shaft of the brushless motor is replaced by a custom one. You will be handed a machined bell and a finished shaft — both are prepared before the session. What is left to you is the disassembly and the press fit, which is still a delicate operation: the motor’s structure is mostly aluminium and quite thin, for weight savings.

Remove the circlip on the shaft with the special pliers. Don’t lose it, nor the brass ring.
Separate the rotor from the stator delicately, by hand.
Press the stock shaft out of the rotor bell.






WarningNever load the bell radially



Press the shaft out very carefully, making sure to never apply forces radially on the bell. Use the manual press with appropriate support below the bell to avoid deforming the dome shape. Do not squeeze the bell with a vice, or even by hand.


Press the sun gear onto the new shaft.






WarningSun gear first — this order cannot be undone



The sun gear goes on while the shaft is still free. Once the shaft is pressed into the bell you can no longer support the shaft properly to press the gear on.


Press the new shaft into the bell, making sure not to press on the dome-shaped part of the bell without appropriate support underneath. It is a tight fit on the bell and a clearance fit through the bearings.







Figure 1: Motor shaft dimensions

title: Module 2 — Motor and transmission shaft
text:
Sensor magnet
The AS5047P encoder you wire up in Module 3 does not touch the shaft. It reads the direction of the magnetic field from a small magnet rotating in front of it, so the magnet has to go on the motor.
Use a 6 × 2.5 mm diametrically magnetised disc magnet. Diametrically magnetised is the part that matters: the poles are across the diameter, not through the thickness, so the field seen by the sensor sweeps through a full rotation as the shaft turns. An ordinary axially magnetised disc of identical size presents the same pole to the sensor all the way round and gives no angle at all.

Drop the magnet into its recess in the 3D-printed bracket. It should sit flat, fully seated, with no rocking.
Centre it on the axis of rotation. The bracket locates it, but check. Keep the magnet concentric with the shaft to within 0.5 mm.
Bond it with a single drop of superglue. One drop is enough.
Turn the assembly through a full revolution by hand and watch the magnet. Any visible wobble means it is off-centre or not seated.







WarningOff-centre magnets are hard to diagnose later



An eccentric magnet may still produces a perfectly plausible angle reading at times.

title: Module 2 — Motor and transmission shaft
text:
Mounting the motor
With the shaft and the magnet done, the motor goes onto the robot. This happens in two stages: motor to bracket, then bracket to plate.

Fix the motor to the vertical 3D-printed nylon bracket using four screws through the mounting holes in the motor base. Don’t over tighten. Check that the rotor still turns freely by hand. Nylon is compliant, and overtightening can pull the bracket out of flat enough to preload the bearings. A motor that spun freely on the bench and feels stiff once bolted down is telling you to back the screws off and retighten more gently.
Mount the bracket to the bottom fuselage plate. Before tightening, check the orientation: the shaft and sun gear must point towards the front of the robot.







ImportantTo be completed by the instructor



Fastener specification for both stages — screw size and length for the motor to the bracket, and the count and size for the bracket to the bottom fuselage plate. Length matters most: screws that are too long reach the stator windings inside the motor.








NoteCheckpoint



Shaft seated with the sun gear on it, the rotor spinning freely by hand with no wobble, the magnet bonded concentric to within 0.5 mm, and the motor bolted to its bracket and mounted on the plate — still turning freely once bolted down.








ImportantTo be prepared by the instructor before the session



Both the bells and the shafts must be prepared ahead of time, one set per student. Neither fits in the session: the lathe work is on thin-walled aluminium that is easy to ruin, and there is not enough machine time for the whole cohort.
Machine the bells. Clamp the bell in the lathe using its stock shaft, then take the propeller horn off by bringing the diameter down to 6 mm and the length to 2.5 mm.






Stock bell







Bring diameter down to 6 mm







Bring the length down to 2.5 mm





Turn the shafts from 4 mm steel rod to the dimensions in Figure 1 — clearance fit through the bearings, tight fit on the bell. The 21.5 mm total assumes the motor and gearbox are separated by a 5.5 mm-thick wall; for a 4 mm wall, shorten the 8.5 mm segment to 7 mm, giving 20 mm overall.
Prepare spares of both — a deformed bell cannot be recovered.

title: FAAV Build Manual
text:
Figure 1: The FAAV3.2
Over the semester your team builds a flapping aerial-aquatic vehicle: a robot that flies, lands on water, swims by flapping the same wings, and takes off again. This manual is the build side of the course. It is sequenced to the weekly modules, and each page covers exactly what you do in that module.

title: FAAV Build Manual
text:
How this manual is organised
Build modules are cumulative and in order. Each one opens with what you are building that day, what to have ready before you arrive, and ends with a checkpoint a TA signs off.
Reference holds the material you consult rather than follow: the parts list, the firmware repositories, the PCB revisions, the CNC guide, and the design notes explaining why the robot is the way it is.

title: FAAV Build Manual
text:
Architecture in one paragraph
One 4S battery (16.8 V max) feeds a custom PCB that steps VBAT down to 5 V to power the flight controller, which in turn generates a 3v3 rail for the sensors on that PCB. Battery power passes through a shunt for current sensing, then out to the ESC. The flight controller commands the ESC over serial. The ESC drives a brushless motor through a 23.04:1 gearbox, and a crank–linkage converts that rotation into wing flapping.

title: Brushless motors
text: Background for Module 2. Not needed at the bench — useful for your report, and for understanding why the motor behaves the way it does when you push it in Module 4.

title: Brushless motors
section: Start with the brushed DC motor
text:
Start with the brushed DC motor
Every result you need for a brushless motor is easier to see in a brushed one first, because the two obey the same electrical physics. The difference is how the windings get switched, not what the machine does once they are.
A DC motor is described by two constants and one resistance. Spinning the rotor induces a back-EMF proportional to speed, and passing current through the windings produces torque proportional to current:
\[U_\text{emf} = \frac{\omega}{k_V} \qquad\qquad \tau = k_T \, I \tag{1}\]
These are the same \(k_V\) and \(k_T\) derived in Module 2 — inverses of each other, not independent choices. The supply voltage splits between the back-EMF and the ohmic drop across the winding resistance \(R\):
\[U = \frac{\omega}{k_V} + R \, I \tag{2}\]
Substitute \(I = \tau / k_T\) and rearrange for torque, and the whole behaviour of the motor falls out as a straight line:
\[\tau = k_T \frac{U}{R} - \frac{k_T}{k_V R}\,\omega \tag{3}\]

Reading the torque–speed line
That line is the motor’s entire steady-state character, and it is fixed by the applied voltage. Two points define it:

Stall torque \(\tau_\text{stall} = k_T U / R\), at \(\omega = 0\). The rotor is held still, there is no back-EMF, and the only thing limiting current is the winding resistance. This is the largest torque the motor can produce and also the fastest way to destroy it — see Thermal limits.
No-load speed \(\omega_0 = k_V U\), at \(\tau = 0\). The rotor spins fast enough that the back-EMF nearly cancels the supply, so almost no current flows.

Everything the motor can do at that voltage lies on the line between them. Mechanical power is \(P = \tau \omega\), the product of a falling line and a rising one, so it is a parabola peaking at half the no-load speed with half the stall torque. Efficiency peaks somewhere else entirely — much closer to \(\omega_0\), because the copper loss that dominates at low speed scales with \(I^2\) while the useful output only scales with \(I\).









NoteThe useful consequence



Raising the voltage shifts the line outwards without changing its slope: more speed and more torque, same trade-off between them. That is why speed control is voltage control, and why a “faster” motor at fixed voltage is a lower-torque one.

title: Brushless motors
section: What changes with a brushless motor
text:
What changes with a brushless motor
In a brushed motor the commutator and brushes are a mechanical switch riding on the rotor: they physically reconnect the windings as it turns, so the current always flows in whichever coil is best placed to produce torque. It works without any electronics at all, and it wears out, arcs, and limits how fast the motor can safely spin.
A BLDC motor deletes that switch. The permanent magnets go on the rotor, the windings stay on the stator in three phases, and an external controller decides which phases to energise based on where the rotor currently is. The motor becomes inseparable from its driver — this is why Module 3 exists, and why the rotor position measurement matters so much.
What this does not change is Equation 3. The torque and speed constants have the same meaning, the line has the same shape, and you size the motor the same way. What changes is that the line is no longer the whole story:









Brushed
Brushless




Commutation
Mechanical, self-acting
Electronic, needs rotor position


Torque–speed line
The real limit
The ideal limit, then clipped by the driver


Wear
Brushes are consumable
Bearings only


Speed ceiling
Brush arcing and bounce
Commutation rate and sensor lag


Torque ripple
Smoothed by many commutator segments
Depends on drive scheme (trapezoidal vs FOC)




The envelope, not the line
The straight line assumes the supply can deliver whatever current the equations ask for. It cannot. At stall, Equation 2 gives \(I = U/R\), and with the sub-ohm winding resistance of a small outrunner that is a number in the hundreds of amps — far beyond both the ESC and the motor itself.
So the driver enforces a current limit, and because \(\tau = k_T I\) that is directly a torque limit. The usable region becomes:

a constant-torque region at low speed, flat at whatever current limit you set, because the ESC is holding current rather than letting the line dictate it;
a corner speed where the back-EMF has risen enough that the supply can no longer push that current;
above it, the original Equation 3 line, falling to \(\omega_0\).

The flat part is not physics, it is a decision. On our robot it is the decision that keeps the motor alive at the low speeds used for swimming, where the torque–speed line alone would happily draw enough current to cook the windings.

title: Brushless motors
text:
Thermal limits
Nothing in Equation 3 knows about heat, which is why the equations cheerfully predict operating points that will destroy the motor in seconds.
Almost all the loss you care about is copper loss in the windings:
\[P_\text{copper} = I^2 R \tag{4}\]
The square is what makes this the binding constraint. Doubling the torque doubles the current and quadruples the heating. A motor comfortable at its rated current will not survive twice that for long, even though the torque equation says it is only a factor of two.
Three practical consequences:

Stall is the worst case, not the best. At \(\omega = 0\) there is maximum current and no rotation, so no airflow and no useful output — all the input power becomes heat in the windings. A motor held at stall can burn out without the shaft moving at all.
Continuous and peak ratings are different numbers. A peak rating assumes seconds; a continuous rating assumes thermal equilibrium. Flapping is a reciprocating load, so the current is far from constant — what matters for heating is the RMS current over the cycle, not the peak you see on the bench supply.
Iron losses grow with speed. Hysteresis and eddy-current losses in the stator scale with electrical frequency, so at the 1700 rad/s discussed in Module 4 the copper is no longer the only thing getting warm.










WarningHeat is cumulative and invisible



Current is the only symptom you can see, and it appears instantly, while the temperature it causes lags behind by tens of seconds. A run that looks fine on the ammeter can still be depositing heat faster than the motor sheds it. When tuning in Module 4, stop and touch the motor.

text:

Everything above is the model. The plot below is where the test-stand measurements go, so you can see how far the straight line actually holds for the motor on your bench.

title: Brushless motors
text:
Why an outrunner
Brushless motors come in two arrangements. An inrunner spins a magnet rotor inside a stationary stator, the familiar shape from a drill. An outrunner inverts it: the stator sits still in the middle and the magnets are carried on a bell that rotates around the outside. Ours is an outrunner — it is the bell you machine and press the shaft into in Module 2.






Figure 1: An outrunner seen from the back. The copper windings are the stator and do not move; the dark magnet segments around the rim are carried on the rotating bell. Note how far out the magnets sit — that radius is the lever arm in Equation 5, and it is the whole reason for this arrangement. Note also that the heat is generated in the middle, wrapped inside the part that spins.



The reason is torque. Torque is force times radius, and in an outrunner the magnets sit at the largest radius the motor’s diameter allows, rather than the smallest:
\[\tau = F \times r \tag{5}\]
The same tangential force from the same windings acts on a longer lever arm. It also leaves room for more magnet poles around the circumference. Together these raise \(k_T\) for a motor of the same mass, which by Equation 1 means a lower KV — more torque per amp, less speed per volt.
That is the right trade for us. The wings need torque at low speed, through a gearbox that is already multiplying by 23.04:1, and the alternative is either a larger reduction or more current for the same result. Two secondary properties help as well:

Rotor inertia. The rotating mass is at a large radius, so the bell has significant inertia and acts as a flywheel. Against a reciprocating flapping load that smooths the speed variation over a cycle. It also means the motor cannot change speed quickly, which is a real cost during transients.
Something to attach to. The bell is a large-diameter rotating surface, which is what makes the shaft press-fit in Module 2 mechanically sensible in the first place.

The costs are real: outrunners spin more slowly for a given voltage, the exposed rotating bell is a hazard and an ingress path, and cooling is worse because the heat-producing stator is wrapped inside the rotor rather than mounted against the case. The last point ties directly back to Thermal limits — an outrunner’s stator sheds heat mainly through its mount, which on our robot is a 3D-printed plate.

title: Design notes
text: Why the robot is built the way it is. Not needed at the bench — useful for your report, and for anyone changing the design.

title: Design notes
text:
Why an FOC ESC
Several ESC solutions were explored for the FAAV concept:

Regular drone ESCs. Hobbyking 12A and EP Aer11 were tested. Both start losing synchronisation at low speed, which is a problem for water propulsion — precisely the regime the robot spends most of its time in.
FOC ESCs tend to be more complex and larger. The G431-ESC1 board is favourable and had already been explored in the lab.

That tradeoff — accepting a larger, more complex driver to get usable low-speed torque control — is the reason Module 3 spends a whole module on the driver.

title: Design notes
text:
Speed ceiling and sensor lag
Maximum speed went from 500 to 1700 rad/s, enough to drive the wings at 10 Hz, through a combination of sensor and MCU changes documented in Module 4. The remaining constraint is sensor lag: above 500–600 rad/s, uncompensated lag shows up as high current draw and noise rather than as a hard speed limit.
Compensation is currently hand-tuned every 100 rad/s with a fitted function used on the robot. Automating this — ramping through the speeds while minimising phase current — is open work.

title: Design notes
text:
Gearbox corrosion
By default the gearbox on the FAAV4 is not waterproof at all, and it is normal for it to fill completely with water once submerged. This was considered acceptable: over more than a year of repeated use in water, including in Lake Geneva, a gearbox was opened and showed no sign of corrosion.
Proper lubrication — a mix of CorrosionX and white lithium grease - help with corrosion problems. The practical procedure is in Module 10.

title: PCB revisions
text:
v2.0 — MIT
The goal of this version was to fix existing functional problems (I²C, pad spacing) and to introduce a new external I²C pad for GPS functionality. It is also designed to function by default with both the newer ESP32S3 chips and NRF52 chips. Improvements in range through WiFi connection are expected. Manufacturing steps are identical to v1.0.

ESP32 compatibility
Hardware and software arrangements were needed for XIAO ESP32S3 compatibility. For software see Software.
Hardware changes: a new PCB housing part allowing SD card removal and reinsertion, a WiFi antenna housing case, and a GPS housing case.
SD card notes

SD cards should be formatted to a specific format (FAT32, believed).
Use non-sharp tweezers to gently extract the SD card from the PCB case — otherwise you risk breaking the card and making it unreadable.
For simultaneous servo and SD card usage, be careful not to use the same pins as on the previous chip for servos; TX and RX are used for SD card communication. You may use the secondary microSD card PCB’s two additional pins.



Waterproofing
The method changes slightly from Module 10. Admittedly it can be vastly improved, but it works:

Insert the assembled PCB, making sure the secondary SD card PCB does not come loose, and that the WiFi antenna is properly inserted.
Insert the USB-C cable into the port, and a microSD card in the relevant slit.
Tape the bottom of the PCB so no silicone escapes when pouring. Pour silicone, using a needle to ensure there are no air bubbles between layers.
When fully cured, the SD card is very hard to remove if the protective section broke off during assembly. It can be salvaged by cutting around three sides of the SD card with a knife and opening it like a trap door, freeing the stuck sections. The trap door can then be sealed with epoxy or more silicone — only on the surface, as you do not want to block the SD card again.

The WiFi antenna should also be potted. Currently the same housing case as for the ESC is used: tape the bottom of the box with Kapton tape, stick the antenna to the bottom of the casing (normally all in sticker form), then pot it with silicone. The silicone layer should be left relatively thin.






NoteThe antenna stops working when wet



It works again once dried. This is expected behaviour, not a fault.




Points for a redesign

Incorrect wiring for pressure sensor — SDA and SCL are swapped.
Cover the vias (currently open vias).
Vias on pads of small SMD components are not optimal for soldering, or just cover the vias.
Increase pad spacing for the cables.
Current sensor: possibly change to a 3.3 V part. Currently a 5 V sensor is used, so current should not exceed \((3.3\,\mathrm{V} - 0.5\,\mathrm{V}) / 0.2\,\mathrm{V/A} = 14\,\mathrm{A}\) without risking damage to the analog ports of the Seeeduino.
UART RX and TX are swapped (resolved)

The robot

The FAAV is a flapping-wing vehicle that operates in air and in water with the same actuation. The build divides into four subsystems, and the modules follow that order:

title: Module 3 — Motor driver, sensor and serial
text:
Electronic Speed Controller
The B-G431B-ESC1 is ST’s reference three-phase motor driver: a complete ESC on one small board, sold as an evaluation kit. Three parts of it matter for this build:

An STM32G431 microcontroller. A 170 MHz Cortex-M4 with hardware floating point. Motor control recomputes the field orientation every control loop. This MCU is the reason we can.
A three-phase inverter with current sensing. Six power MOSFETs drive the three motor phases, and shunt resistors on the low side report the current actually flowing in each. That measurement is what turns “spin the motor” into torque control. You cannot regulate a current you cannot see.







Figure 3: The power stage of the B-G431B-ESC1. The six MOSFETs are the large flat packages, arranged as three half-bridges — one per motor phase, each with a high-side and a low-side switch. The three copper tabs on the left are the U, V and W outputs you solder the motor to below, and the grey block behind is the heatsink.




A detachable ST-Link programmer (the daughterboard). The small daughter board is how we program the MCU over USB, and it also carries a serial port back to your laptop. When snapped-off, the MCU cannot be reprogramed without physically resoldering it.

It also brings out a hall/encoder connector (J8), a CAN transceiver and a potentiometer input, none of which we use as intended. In this build J8 gets repurposed for serial, and the encoder arrives on SPI instead. Both of those reworks are below. The board is rated well above what the wing motor draws, so current is not the constraint here.
crumbs: Module 3 --- Motor driver, sensor and serial

title: Module 3 — Motor driver, sensor and serial
text:
Angular sensor

Why the motor needs an encoder
Field-Oriented Control works by holding the stator’s magnetic field roughly 90° ahead of the rotor’s magnets, which is the orientation that produces the most torque per amp. To place the field there, the controller has to know where the rotor is right now.
Ordinary drone ESCs infer this from back-EMF, i.e the voltage the spinning rotor induces in the phase that is not currently being driven (?@eq-bemf in Module 2). That voltage is proportional to speed, so as the motor slows the signal sinks into the noise and the estimate falls apart. This causes loss of synchronisation at low speed described in Design notes. The AS5047P removes the guess. It measures the field of the magnet bonded to the shaft end and reports the absolute angle — valid at standstill just as much as at 15 000 rpm, and correct immediately at power-on with no homing move.


What SPI is, and why we run it at 10 MHz
The AS5047P reports angle over SPI, a four-wire synchronous bus: the controller drives the clock (SCLK), data goes out on MOSI and comes back on MISO, and CS selects the chip. Transfer speed is limited only by how fast the two ends can shift bits. We use SPI because it offers 10 MHz communication. The reason speed matters is that the angle has to be re-read every single control loop, and a stale angle is gad: the controller ends up placing the stator field where the rotor was, not where it is. That error shows up as wasted current and audible noise. The same 10 MHz clock is why the wiring has to stay short, see below.


Wiring it to the board
There is no SPI link exposed directly on the ESC board. The solution is to use the SPI3 bus, exposed through a few hardware modifications and matching software changes. Figure 1 shows the four signals in context, including the MOSI tap on R14.



Table 1: SPI3 connections on the G431. * Solder onto the outward side of the resistor.

MISO

WarningKeep the SPI cables under 8 cm



Cables between encoder and ESC need to be less than 8 cm. At 10 MHz longer runs start corrupting angle readings, and the symptom is a motor that behaves erratically rather than a sensor that obviously fails.


Next, use M2 screws to mount the encoder on the 3D printed bracket that sits around the motor. Check that the distance between sensor and magnet is 0.5 mm, and centered.

text:
How to program the ESC
With the encoder and motor connected to the ESC, we can start programing the ESC! The daughterboard is already connected to the ESC MCU. We can program it, but we cannot communicate between our laptop and the ESC. Out of the box that happens via Serial2, but we will reuse those GPIOs for the encoder connections. In that case we must connect Serial1 (on the MCU) to the daughterboard:

Disconnect USART2 and connect USART1: remove R23 and R24 on the daughter board (desolder).
Solder wires to the now-free pins of R23/R24 - the pads closer to U3, further away from the USB port. Connect the wire from R23 to the pad for hall sensor 2 (PB7), and the wire from R24 to the pad for hall sensor 1 (PB6) on J8.
Remap the pins in software for SPI use: in platformio.ini via build_flags, and by overwriting the WEAK PinMaps in pinmap_custom.h. See commit 18520ac on GitHub for details.

text:
Commanding and monitoring
This is a high-level summary of the SimpleFOC communication docs. Communication with the ESC is over serial, either via the ST-Link programmer (the small attached board that we will use for now) or via a separate microcontroller board (that will come next week).
Once serial communication is established, you interact with the ESC through the commander, a practical interface for setting and getting values (instructions). Ask the commander for available commands with ?. Commands available:







Command
Effect




M
Full motor configuration


F
Get the main loop frequency


L
Turn the onboard LED on and off (useful as a comms check)


T
Set the target value — rad, rad/s or N/m depending on control mode


W
Watchdog on/off. If no new target arrives for 1 s, target is set to zero. On by default


R
R0/R1 disable/enable a linear ramp when changing setpoint. RD1000 sets ramp duration to 1000 ms (default 1000 ms). Off by default









WarningCareful when changing control mode



T means something different in each mode, position, velocity, or torque. Sending a velocity setpoint while in torque mode will do something you did not intend, with the wings attached. BE VERY CAREFUL ABOUT THIS.








NoteCheckpoint



Commander responds to ? over serial at 115200 baud, L toggles the onboard LED, the sensor returns a plausible angle through a full manual rotation, and the motor spins under a T command.








ImportantTo be prepared by the instructor before the session



Prepare a power source 15V 5A over USB-C.

text:
Crank and linkage






Figure 2: The transmission, exploded, with the length that matters and the material for each part. Follow it left to right: the gearbox output turns the crank, the crank drives the linkage, and the linkage swings the inter-wing gear. The 34° up and −26° down at the right are where the 60° flapping amplitude comes from — it is set here, by these lengths, and cannot be changed in software.



The dimensions called out in Figure 2 are the ones you cut to:



Table 1: Crank–linkage dimensions






Crank-linkage dimensions




Crank radius
4.5 mm


Linkage length
24 mm


Crank–linkage shaft diameter
4 mm


Bearing, crank side
10×4×4


Bearing, wing side
8×3×4 flanged






Both the crank and linkage are CNC-cut in a 5 mm aluminium plate.
Once cut:

Carefully tap an M3 thread. Use cutting oil and make sure to break off the chips.






WarningThis thread carries high forces



It must be done carefully, keeping the alignment between hole and tap.


Press the bearings into the linkage. They may need to be bonded with metal glue if the press fit is not good enough.
Join the crank and linkage with a short 4 mm shaft, cut to 9.5 mm. The bearing is kept from coming out with a pointy indent on the shaft end. (To be improved.)







WarningAlignment of the linkage, perpendicular to the shafts, is extremely important



An offset of 1 mm is sufficient to destroy the crank-link in a few strokes.


Figure 3 shows how the four shafts for the FAAV3.2 should be manufactured. Nothing exotic, but they need to be accurate.








Transmission, top view







Shaft dimensions






Figure 3



The 3 mm shafts are pressed through the two gears’ centre holes. Should be a mildly tight fit at minimum, otherwise glue the shaft. Same for the linkage shaft (also 3 mm).
Between the gears, a clearance of 0.4 mm (inter-axis spacing of 25.4 mm) ensures proper operation without too much backlash.






Transmission assembled







Transmission, second view











NoteCheckpoint



Frame assembled, crank–linkage rotating freely through a full cycle with no binding, linkage visibly perpendicular to the shafts, and gear backlash checked. Flapping shown at 1-5 Hz.

title: Module 7 — Wing fabrication
text: Week of Oct 26 · Paired lecture: Swimming robots II

title: Module 7 — Wing fabrication
text:
What you build today
Both wings: carbon skeleton, membrane cut to the geometry you chose in Module 6, bonded and stitched at the load-bearing points.

title: Module 7 — Wing fabrication
text:
Before you arrive







Parts
Carbon rods and strips, wing roots, 2× nylon adapters per wing, ripstop nylon membrane, 3M tape, superglue, thread


Tools
Cutting mat, steel rule, scalpel, needle, printed full-size template of your geometry


Bring
Your Module 6 geometry, printed 1:1

title: Module 7 — Wing fabrication
text:
Wing roots
The wing roots are carbon, drilled to mate with the gears from Module 5.






Figure 1: Wing root parts and spar stock

title: Module 7 — Wing fabrication
text:
Building the wing
The whole wing is built over the printed pattern, working from the leading edge outwards. Everything is cut oversize and trimmed to the outline at the very end — margin is easy to remove and impossible to add back.

Decide on the shape and print the pattern on paper. Print it 1:1 — check the scale before you cut anything, by measuring a known dimension on the printout against a rule. Printer drivers scale to fit by default, and a pattern that came out at 97% quietly discards the geometry you chose in Module 6.
Cut two membranes with a 3 cm margin all round the pattern. Use the ripstop nylon listed in Parts.
Bond the leading edge. Lay a strip of 3M tape along the leading-edge region of the membrane, press the leading-edge rod down onto the tape, and wrap the membrane around the rod. This joint carries the highest load of any on the wing — everything downstream pulls against it.
Lay out the carbon strips. Cut each to approximate length plus 3 cm, position them on the membrane over the pattern, and bond them with superglue.
Stitch the strips down, at minimum at every intersection point and at the extremities. Superglue alone will peel off the membrane under repeated flapping; the stitches are what keep the skeleton attached once the glue starts to fail.
Trim the excess beyond the outline with a blade, cutting on the mat.







Strips laid out and bonded over the template







Trimming the membrane to the outline





Repeat for the second wing, and remember that it is flipped.






Figure 2: Completed wing pair

title: Module 7 — Wing fabrication
text:
Assembly

Mount each wing in its wing root using the two nylon adapters.
Mount the wing roots in the robot, onto the gears from Module 5.
Check that it flaps. Run it slowly first and watch both wings through a full cycle before going any faster.







WarningBoth wings must match



Asymmetry between left and right shows up as a roll bias that may not be possible to correct later. See Module 11 for trimming out. Weigh both wings and compare spar positions against the template before bonding.








ImportantTo be completed by the instructor



Still missing from the procedure above:

Which 3M tape — the parts list says VHB, the width and where exactly it lands on the leading edge are not recorded
Spar layup: rod and strip diameters, and where the diagonals attach
What to stitch with — thread type and stitch spacing
Numerical tolerance between left and right wing, for the check below









NoteCheckpoint



Both wings complete, matched in mass and geometry, mounted in their roots and fitted to the robot, and flapping through a full cycle without binding.

Before you arrive

Read
This page and PCB revisions

title: Module 9 — Flight controller, PCB and dry testing
text:
Electronic architecture
One 4S (max 16.8 V) battery is connected to a custom PCB that steps VBAT down to 5 V to power the flight controller. The flight controller generates a 3v3 rail to power the sensors on the custom PCB. Battery power goes through a shunt for sensing on the custom PCB, then back out to power the ESC. The flight controller sends commands to the ESC over serial.
crumbs: Module 9 --- Flight controller, PCB and dry testing

text:
Flight controller






Figure 1: Microcontroller in its waterproofing box



Firmware lives in FAAV-Flight-Controller (ESP32, FreeRTOS tasks). See Software for older variants.

title: Module 9 — Flight controller, PCB and dry testing
text:
Assembling the PCB
As of April 2026 the current board is v3.0: 4 layers, 21 × 28.5 mm, 34 components. The complete BOM is in the Manufacturing/Assembly folder of the FAAV-PCB-v3 repository.
The simplest way to assemble a FAAV PCB is with a stencil, solder paste applied with a cutter blade, then reflow on the hotplate.






Tape blank PCBs around the PCB to assemble







Align the stencil on top and tape it, making sure it sits flat











Wipe down solder paste with a blade in one firm pass







Place the assembled PCB on the hot plate
crumbs: Module 9 --- Flight controller, PCB and dry testing

title: Module 9 — Flight controller, PCB and dry testing
text:
Taking the PCB into operation
Once assembled, solder power wires for VBAT and GND at the input side of the board. Follow these steps before powering the PCB for the first time:

Check that there is no short circuit between GND and 5V / 3.3V / VBAT.
Connect a 15 V supply with a 100 mA current limit to the battery pads and check that it does not draw excessive current.
Check with a multimeter that the buck regulator outputs 5 V from the 15 V input. The MCU should be on by then.

With the MCU powered, flash your test firmware and check the connection to all sensors. Table 1 gives the I²C addresses.



Table 1: I²C addresses





Component
I²C address (bin)
I²C address (hex)




Pressure sensor
0b1110110
0x76


IMU
0b1101000
0x68


INA228 power monitor
0b0101000
0x40






Verify:

Voltage, current and temperature readings from the INA228
IMU readings
Pressure sensor readings
RGB LED control

Once all the hardware on the board is validated, solder the power wires at the output side of the board to the ESC, and the UART wires.






WarningTX to RX



The TX output of the PCB has to be connected to the RX pin of the ESC, and vice versa.
crumbs: Module 9 --- Flight controller, PCB and dry testing

title: Module 9 — Flight controller, PCB and dry testing
text:
Connectors
The waterproof connector is the JST 8-pin 08R-JWPF-VSLE-D / 08T-JWPF-VSLE-D. All pins marked _b are used for balancing the battery during recharge. For use on the robot, connect at least Vbat and GND; to allow higher currents, connect Vbat_b and GND_b as well.






WarningSeal the unused cable slots



Do not forget to seal the back of the connector for the unused cable slots — this is a water ingress path straight into the electronics.








Figure 2: Connector wiring scheme. Left: battery connector. Right: connector on the robot / for recharging the battery.

title: Module 9 — Flight controller, PCB and dry testing
text:
Dry testing






ImportantTo be written by the instructor



The dry-test protocol is course material, not in the guide. Needed: what the robot is mounted on while flapping in air, the flap frequency sweep, what is measured, the wireless control setup students reprogram to, and abort criteria.








NoteCheckpoint — TA sign-off



PCB validated against all four sensor checks, flight controller commanding the ESC over serial, and a supervised flapping run in air.

title: Module 11 — Wet testing
text: Week of Nov 23 · Paired lecture: Fixed-wing flyers

title: Module 11 — Wet testing
text:
What you do today
Immersion, underwater runs, wing trim, and control tuning in water — the regime the whole transmission was designed around.

title: Module 11 — Wet testing
text:
Before you arrive



Bring
Fully waterproofed robot from Module 10, charged 4S pack, spare crank–linkage shaft


Read
This page, and your notes from Module 4

title: Module 11 — Wet testing
text:
Pre-immersion checks

Static immersion test from Module 10 passed, robot opened and inspected dry
Connector back-shell sealed on all unused slots
Gearbox lubricated with CorrosionX and white lithium grease
Watchdog enabled on the ESC (W) — target drops to zero if commands stop
Robot floats level







WarningLow speed is where hobby ESCs fail



Water propulsion runs the motor in exactly the regime where synchronisation is lost. If the drive stutters underwater, stop and check sensor lag compensation before increasing current — see Module 4.








ImportantTo be written by the instructor



The wet-test protocol is course material and has no counterpart in the manufacturing guide. Needed:

Tank or venue, and supervision requirements
Run profile: depth, duration, flap frequency sweep
What is logged, and how it is retrieved — SD card handling on a potted board is not trivial, see PCB revisions
How wing trim is adjusted, and against what reference
Cost of transport measurement procedure, since it is scored in Module 12
Recovery and abort procedure









NoteCheckpoint — TA sign-off



A completed underwater run with logged data, no water ingress on inspection afterwards, and a recorded cost-of-transport measurement.
